section_summary: This section centers on U.S. exports of strategic materials and industrial technology to Japan in 1940, especially scrap iron, petroleum products, aviation gasoline components, machine tools, aluminum oxide, and chemical supplies. It documents growing public and congressional pressure for an embargo, State Department explanations that existing law offered little authority to prohibit trade, and the emergence of national-defense export-control legislation. The papers also record confidential consultations with businesses over Japanese purchases, credit requests, and the withholding of technology for producing high-octane aviation fuel.

subfiles.title: List of Papers: Army Equipment and Supplies—Japan
subfiles.about: Indexes later correspondence concerning exports of strategic materials and supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: These pages continue a file-level list of papers for 1941, summarizing congressional correspondence, diplomatic reports, and interdepartmental memoranda about exports to Japan. Subjects include scrap iron, petroleum, machinery, bearings, cobalt, tungsten, cotton, and other strategic commodities from the United States and Latin America.

subfiles.title: Japanese requests for credit on scrap purchases
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese buyers were seeking extended credit from American scrap dealers.
subfiles.summary: Jansen says Japan fell from first to third among buyers of American scrap, possibly for lack of funds; Yost says businesses are advised that Japan's finances make credit unwise.
keywords: Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce

subfiles.title: Japanese commercial interests seek credit for oil shipments
subfiles.about: Reports concerted Japanese efforts to obtain credit from major American oil companies.
subfiles.summary: Embassy learns Japanese interests press American oil companies for credit; Standard Oil of California is paid only after tankers reach Japan, and no credit for military purchases.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Tokyo telegram on oil credit
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the embassy's report on Japanese requests for credit on oil shipments.
subfiles.summary: Paraphrase: Japanese commercial interests seek credit from American oil companies; Standard Oil of California gives open credit commercially but none for military and naval purchases.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products suspends Japanese cracking-plant work
subfiles.from: L. M. Healy, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.about: Provides the cable suspending work on cracking and aviation-gasoline projects for Japanese clients.
subfiles.summary: Universal Oil Products cabled Saneyoshi that critical conditions require its facilities for domestic cracking and aviation gasoline, so it suspended work for Mitsui and Fujinagata.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Universal Oil Products letter
subfiles.about: Acknowledges information about suspended sales of cracking plants to Japanese firms.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks the company for reporting its action on Mitsui and Japan Gasoline Company projects.

subfiles.title: Greene urges action against war-supply exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges presidential attention to continuing American supplies of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene, for the American Committee for Non-Participation, asks the President to consider action consistent with its embargo campaign; letter degraded.

subfiles.title: “Bring on the Embargo”
subfiles.about: Editorially advocates a complete embargo on American war supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Clipping 'Bring on the Embargo': American scrap iron sustains Japan's China war and may be used against Americans; calls for an embargo now that the treaty is abrogated.

subfiles.title: Wallgren forwards Cook's anti-export appeal
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's request that the United States stop supplying Japan with war materials.
subfiles.summary: Wallgren forwards L. D. Cook's letter and asks for information on ending war-material shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cook asks Wallgren to oppose war-material exports
subfiles.about: Calls for a long-term American policy ending shipments of finished or raw war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cook argues continued supplies enable Japan to arm and threaten world peace, in a nonpartisan appeal.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Wallgren on legal authority for an embargo
subfiles.about: Explains that new legislation would be needed to prohibit most exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull stated that no existing statute authorized an embargo on commodities exported to Japan except tin-plate scrap and helium gas. He noted that Representative Charles H. Leavy had forwarded an identical Cook letter and returned Wallgren's enclosure.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment concerning cracking-plant plans
subfiles.about: Acknowledges cable information about Japanese cracking-plant plans.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Universal Oil Products for the Saneyoshi-Halle exchange on cracking plants in Japan.

subfiles.title: Leavy forwards Cook's anti-export appeal
subfiles.about: Submits a constituent letter for State Department consideration and comment.
subfiles.summary: Leavy forwards Leo Cook's letter, asking that its request be met if possible and information on the Department's action.

subfiles.title: Cook asks Leavy to oppose war-material exports
subfiles.about: Urges Leavy to press for an end to American war-material supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cook's essentially identical letter to Leavy on exports enabling Japan to arm and threaten peace.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Leavy on legal authority for an embargo
subfiles.about: Explains the absence of statutory authority for a broad embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull said that existing law did not authorize a general embargo, apart from tin-plate scrap and helium gas. He mentioned Wallgren's identical submission and returned Cook's letter.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: blending agents and crude petroleum
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum of a conversation with E. B. Badger about exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: memorandum on blending agents and crude petroleum, from a talk with E. B. Badger on exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: Navy requisition of machine tools
subfiles.from: Department of State, Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum about Navy requisitioning of machine tools ordered for foreign countries.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Commander Carney of the Navy called about machine tools already on order for foreign purchasers.

subfiles.title: Extracts from Republican members of Congress on a proposed Japan embargo
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Compiles congressional statements favoring restrictions on war-material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Harry B. Price left this compilation with the Department as evidence of Republican congressional support for an embargo. The quotations range from unqualified support to cautious backing conditioned on executive approval or avoidance of war, and also note favorable responses from several Democratic senators.

subfiles.title: American scrap exports and Japanese naval construction
subfiles.from: Harry B. Price, American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Argues that American scrap iron and machinery made Japan's naval expansion possible.
subfiles.summary: The release cites Commerce Department statistics showing that Japan received more American iron and steel scrap than all other countries combined during 1934–1939. It connects those supplies to Japanese naval construction, war industries, and the war in China, and supports pending Pittman-Schwellenbach legislation.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs returns draft reply on Greene proposal
subfiles.about: Transmits a draft reply for General Watson to send Roger S. Greene.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs returns a draft reply to Greene's May 17 letter, with the original letters to General Watson and the President.

subfiles.title: Protocol requests draft reply for General Watson
subfiles.about: Requests a draft response to Roger S. Greene for General Watson's signature.
subfiles.summary: Summerlin asks Far Eastern Affairs to prepare a reply for General Watson on Greene's proposal for broad presidential export-control powers.

subfiles.title: Watson asks Summerlin for a reply to Greene
subfiles.about: Requests a draft reply to Roger S. Greene's attached letter.
subfiles.summary: Watson asks Summerlin to prepare a response to Greene's proposal on presidential control of war-material exports.

subfiles.title: Greene forwards his proposal to General Watson
subfiles.about: Asks Watson to bring an enclosed export-control proposal to the President's attention.
subfiles.summary: Greene, assuming the President is too busy, asks Watson to present his letter on an important matter.

subfiles.title: Greene proposes broad presidential export-control authority
subfiles.about: Proposes legislation allowing the President to withhold basic war materials and equipment from export.
subfiles.summary: Greene congratulated Roosevelt on his defense address and described his committee's campaign to restrict supplies to Japan. Because of the expanding European war, he proposed broader national-security legislation giving the President discretion to prohibit exports while permitting transactions compatible with American interests.

subfiles.title: Summerlin transmits White House correspondence to Greene
subfiles.about: Forwards the response to Greene and returns his papers.
subfiles.summary: Summerlin sends Greene the reply prepared through White House and State routing, with file material enclosed.

subfiles.title: White House reply to Greene on export-control legislation
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Greene's proposal and points to congressional consideration of national-defense legislation.
subfiles.summary: White House reply notes Greene's request for authority to withhold war materials and avoids commitment, noting Congress was considering defense measures.

subfiles.title: Thomas forwards Myers's protest against exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests information for a constituent about American shipments of scrap iron and munitions to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Thomas forwards Ruth Myers's protest and asks for information on scrap iron and munitions exports.

subfiles.title: Myers urges diversion of supplies from Japan to the Allies
subfiles.about: Demands an end to exports aiding Japan's war in China and urges support for France and Britain.
subfiles.summary: Myers condemns shipments to Japan and argues informal State pressure could stop them and aid France and England instead, citing Peffer.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Thomas on export authority and H.R. 9850
subfiles.about: Explains existing legal limits and notes pending national-defense export legislation.
subfiles.summary: Hull repeated that current law did not authorize a broad embargo on exports to Japan. He added that H.R. 9850 would empower the President to prohibit or curtail exports of commodities essential to national defense and returned Myers's letter.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference: credits for cotton and other nonmilitary supplies
subfiles.about: Points to a telegram about extending credit for cotton and other nonmilitary supplies to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Grew's conversation with a prominent Japanese on credit for raw cotton and other nonmilitary supplies.

subfiles.title: Associated Ethyl reports May shipment to Japan
subfiles.to: Secretary of State, attention Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Reports a shipment of ethyl fluid and tetraethyl lead to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Associated Ethyl shipped one hundred drums of ethyl fluid, 47,300 pounds of tetraethyl lead, to Japan on the Tosan Maru in May; none to the USSR.

subfiles.title: Yost acknowledges Associated Ethyl report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report of ethyl-fluid exports to Japan and none to the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Goux for the May shipment report and the statement of no Soviet shipments.

subfiles.title: White House referral of Coolidge letter
subfiles.about: Refers E. B. Coolidge's letter to the State Department for consideration and acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: White House sends Coolidge's letter to State for consideration and acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Coolidge opposes profiting from scrap exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Declines to profit from Montana scrap sales and advocates comprehensive controls on war materials.
subfiles.summary: Coolidge says Montana, Wyoming and Idaho have 50,000-100,000 tons of scrap sellable to Japan but considers it unpatriotic; urges an embargo covering steel, copper, oil, cotton and all war materials, including to Italy.

subfiles.title: Yost replies to Coolidge on embargo authority
subfiles.about: States that new legislation would be needed to embargo the commodities Coolidge listed.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Coolidge no statute then authorized embargoing the named commodities.

subfiles.title: Eddy asks about American industrial assistance to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests correction or confirmation of reports about American aircraft, steel, and material exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Eddy asks if American firms operate aircraft plants or supply rights and steel mills in Japan, and criticizes high-test gasoline, scrap, steel and copper exports.

subfiles.title: State Department answers Eddy's industrial questions
subfiles.about: Clarifies American industrial interests in Japan and explains the absence of prohibitory legislation.
subfiles.summary: Green says no American company controlled Japanese aircraft subsidiaries, though some sold manufacturing rights; an American firm sold an idle plant; existing law did not prohibit such transactions or exports.

subfiles.title: Ward forwards a constituent petition against scrap exports
subfiles.about: Requests State Department comment on constituents' opposition to scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ward forwards a petition from Ridgely, Maryland residents against scrap exports and asks the Department's comments.

subfiles.title: Ridgely residents oppose scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.from: Nellie M. Dragoo, Lulu E. Bartlett, Lloyd C. Young, Helen Young, Martha Royer, and Wayne Royer
subfiles.about: Asks Ward to use his influence against sending scrap iron to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Six Ridgely constituents signed the short appeal. Their sole request was for Ward to oppose continued scrap-iron shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Hull replies to Ward on scrap-export controls
subfiles.about: Explains that only materials designated as essential to national defense could be controlled under the new authority.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledged Ward's constituent letter advocating an embargo on scrap iron. He stated that no statute authorized prohibition of commodities other than those designated by the Administrator of Export Control as essential to national defense, and returned the petition.

subfiles.title: Price sends committee memorandum on export-control developments
subfiles.about: Encloses a committee memorandum reporting legislative progress and opposing appeasement of Japan.
subfiles.summary: Price sends Hamilton a committee memorandum on export-control developments, hoping it credits supporters and argues soundly against appeasing Japan.

subfiles.title: Progress report and action program against arming Japan
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Reports passage of presidential export-control authority and mobilizes supporters against appeasing Japan.
subfiles.summary: Circular credits public pressure with Section 6 of pending defense legislation allowing the President to curtail exports; urges using it against Japan and aiding China; rejects Japan rapprochement as Munich-like appeasement.

subfiles.title: Hamilton acknowledges committee memorandum
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the committee's June 17 memorandum.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Price's June 19 letter and committee memorandum.

subfiles.title: Japanese request for bids on 150,000 drums of aviation gasoline
subfiles.about: Records interdepartmental advice to delay responding to a very large Japanese aviation-gasoline inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Captain Schuirmann: Standard Oil of New Jersey was asked to bid on 150,000 drums of aviation gasoline worth over seven million dollars; Hornbeck, Hamilton and Green favored stalling until Congress passed export authority.

subfiles.title: Navy concern over aviation-gasoline drum exports
subfiles.about: Records Navy objections to exporting large numbers of steel drums with aviation gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Navy would stall on the Japanese gasoline request but not let many drums leave; Hornbeck said State would favor Navy action preventing export of considerable containers.

subfiles.title: Threatened Japan Gasoline Company suit against Universal Oil Products
subfiles.about: Reports threatened litigation over Universal's suspension of high-octane gasoline-plant plans.
subfiles.summary: Halle says a Japan Gasoline Company attorney served a summons over Universal's failure to complete 100-octane plant plans; Universal acted in cooperation with Department policy.

subfiles.title: Union Carbide inquiry about ethylene dichloride
subfiles.about: Records advice on a proposed sale of ethylene dichloride to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: Union Carbide asks about selling one hundred tons of ethylene dichloride to Japan; Yost finds it outside existing moral embargoes though possibly restricted by pending legislation.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of memorandum on ethylene dichloride
subfiles.about: Duplicates the memorandum concerning Union Carbide's proposed Japanese sale.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Stewart's inquiry about selling one hundred tons of ethylene dichloride to Japanese interests. It again records that the chemical fell outside existing moral embargoes, although future legislation might affect exports.

subfiles.title: Aluminum oxide deemed subject to the moral embargo
subfiles.about: Records advice that aluminum oxide exports to Japan were covered by the moral embargo.
subfiles.summary: Aluminum oxide exports to Japan were advised as subject to the moral embargo and possibly restricted by pending legislation.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products reports further Miike cable exchange
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese demands for completion of Miike drawings and Universal's refusal to resume work.
subfiles.summary: Saneyoshi demanded immediate delivery of Miike drawings; Universal replied work was unavoidably suspended given the critical international situation.

subfiles.title: Protective clause in Standard-Vacuum blending-agent bid
subfiles.about: Records a company's proposed contractual protection against future restrictions on blending-agent exports.
subfiles.summary: Standard-Vacuum's Coe wants a nondelivery clause for a Japanese blending-agent bid; Yost says no restriction exists and no objection, though policy could change.

subfiles.title: Advice on a constituent's proposed steel business with Japan
subfiles.about: Records guidance given to Senator Guffey's secretary about a steel transaction offered by Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck advises a constituent's proposed steel business with Japan is not illegal or under a moral embargo, but credit sales are discouraged and licensing is likely; suggests consulting Stettinius or Knudsen.

subfiles.title: Navy instructions on machine tools for export
subfiles.from: Assistant Secretary of the Navy, Shore Establishments Division
subfiles.about: Directs Navy experts to help Customs identify machine tools needed for American defense and withhold their export.
subfiles.summary: Navy directive on machine tools for export: advise Customs which tools are essential to defense production, allow less useful items and curtail critical ones pending legislation, avoiding restrictions beyond defense needs.

subfiles.title: McCormack forwards veterans' protest against scrap-metal exports
subfiles.about: Transmits a veterans' association letter opposing scrap-metal shipments to belligerent countries, including Japan.
subfiles.summary: McCormack forwards Harry Ginsberg's veterans' protest against scrap-metal exports for the Secretary's information.

subfiles.title: 101st Infantry veterans launch drive against scrap-metal exports
subfiles.about: Announces a veterans' campaign to halt large scrap-metal shipments to belligerent countries, including Japan.
subfiles.summary: 101st Infantry B Company veterans, mostly wounded, launch a drive against large scrap-metal exports, citing American security and youth.
